# Exercise 1: importing a CSV in two ways

1. *Import the file twice, once with base R and once with `readr`.*

   Base R has `read.csv()`, the `readr` package has `read_csv()`:

```{r message=FALSE}
air_quality_base <- read.csv("data/Air_Quality.csv")

library(readr)
air_quality <- read_csv("data/Air_Quality.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

2. *Inspect what you imported with `head()`, `tail()`, `dim()`, and `glimpse()` from `dplyr`.
   How many rows and columns are there?*

   16,122 rows and 12 columns:

```{r}
dim(air_quality)
head(air_quality[, c("Name", "Geo Place Name", "Time Period", "Data Value")])
```

```{r message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
glimpse(air_quality)
```

   The same indicator appears in many rows, once per area and per time period.

3. *Compare `names(air_quality_base)` with `names(air_quality)`. The file has a column called
   `Unique ID`, with a space in the name. What did each function do with that name, and how do
   you refer to the column afterwards?*

```{r}
names(air_quality_base)
names(air_quality)
```

   `read.csv()` repairs the names and turns spaces into dots: `Unique ID` becomes `Unique.ID`,
   so you write `air_quality_base$Unique.ID`. `read_csv()` keeps the original names, so a name
   with a space needs backticks:

```{r}
head(air_quality$`Unique ID`, 3)
```

   Neither is wrong, but you need to know which one you are using.

4. *Compare `class(air_quality_base)` with `class(air_quality)`. What is the difference between
   the two objects?*

```{r}
class(air_quality_base)
class(air_quality)
```

   `read.csv()` returns a `data.frame`, `read_csv()` returns a `tibble`: it prints ten rows
   instead of all of them and shows the type of every column under its name. A tibble is still
   a data frame, which you can see from `data.frame` in its class.

5. *`read_csv()` printed a message about column specifications, `read.csv()` printed nothing.
   Which behaviour do you prefer when you open a file for the first time, and why?*

   The message, for a file you do not know: a column of numbers that was read as text shows up
   immediately instead of three steps later.

# Exercise 2: column types

1. *Print the full specification with `spec(air_quality)`. Which columns came out as
   `col_double()` and which as `col_character()`?*

```{r}
spec(air_quality)
```

   Four columns were guessed as `col_double()`, the two IDs, the join ID and `Data Value`. The
   rest are `col_character()`.

2. *`Start_Date` contains dates such as `06/01/2013`, but it was not read as a date. Why can
   the parser not recognise it, and what would the file have to look like for `readr` to guess
   a date by itself?*

```{r}
head(air_quality$Start_Date, 3)
```

   `readr` guesses dates only in the ISO format, `YYYY-MM-DD`. `06/01/2013` is ambiguous: 1
   June 2013 in the American convention, 6 January 2013 in the European one. Rather than pick
   one, `readr` leaves the column as text. With `2013-06-01` in the file it would have been
   parsed as a date without help.

3. *State the type yourself with `col_types = cols(Start_Date = col_date(format =
   "%m/%d/%Y"))`. Check the class of the column, then run `range()` on it. Which period does
   the data cover? Run `range()` on the text version too, and explain the difference.*

```{r}
air_quality_dates <- read_csv(
  "data/Air_Quality.csv",
  col_types = cols(Start_Date = col_date(format = "%m/%d/%Y"))
)

class(air_quality_dates$Start_Date)
range(air_quality_dates$Start_Date)
```

   The data covers January 2005 to June 2020. On the text version the answer is different:

```{r}
range(air_quality$Start_Date)
```

   Strings are sorted alphabetically, so the smallest is `"01/01/2005"` and the largest
   `"12/31/2015"`: a string starting with `12/` sorts after one starting with `06/`, whatever
   the year follows. Neither value is the first or the last date in the data. The answer looks
   plausible and is wrong.

4. *Why is it better to fix a type at import than to convert the column afterwards?*

   Every later step inherits the type, and a date stored as text cannot be sorted, subtracted
   or plotted on a time axis. Stating the type also records, in the script, what you expect the
   file to contain: the day the provider changes the format, the import fails instead of
   quietly producing `NA`.

# Exercise 3: select what you need and write it back

1. *`Name` holds the indicator that was measured. List the distinct values with
   `unique(air_quality$Name)`. How many are there?*

   Nineteen, from ozone to traffic density:

```{r}
length(unique(air_quality$Name))
unique(air_quality$Name)
```

2. *Keep the rows measuring fine particulate matter in the winter of 2008-09 in Lower
   Manhattan, with `subset()` and `&`. How many rows are left, and what is the measured value?*

```{r}
pm25_winter <- subset(air_quality,
                      Name == "Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5)" &
                      `Time Period` == "Winter 2008-09" &
                      `Geo Place Name` == "Lower Manhattan")

dim(pm25_winter)
pm25_winter$`Data Value`
```

   One row: in winter 2008-09, fine particulate matter in Lower Manhattan was measured at
   15.79 mcg/m³. Use `&`, not `&&`: `&&` looks only at the first element and returns one
   `TRUE` or `FALSE`, which keeps either everything or nothing.

3. *Save the result as `airquality_manhattan.csv` with `write_csv()`, then open the file in a
   text editor.*

```{r eval=FALSE}
write_csv(pm25_winter, "data/airquality_manhattan.csv")
```

   The file holds a header line with the twelve column names and one line of values.
   `write_csv()` writes UTF-8 and, unlike `write.csv()`, adds no column of row numbers. For the
   number alone, use
   `writeLines(as.character(pm25_winter$"Data Value"), "data/airquality_manhattan.txt")`.

4. *Now keep every measurement of fine particulate matter in Lower Manhattan, for all time
   periods, and save it the same way. If you read `Start_Date` as a date in Exercise 2, sort
   the series by date first.*

   Dropping the condition on the time period leaves the whole series for that neighbourhood:

```{r}
pm25_all <- subset(air_quality,
                   Name == "Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5)" &
                   `Geo Place Name` == "Lower Manhattan")

dim(pm25_all)
```

```{r}
pm25_sorted <- pm25_all[order(as.Date(pm25_all$Start_Date, format = "%m/%d/%Y")), ]
head(pm25_sorted[, c("Time Period", "Start_Date", "Data Value")], 4)
```

```{r eval=FALSE}
write_csv(pm25_sorted, "data/airquality_manhattan_all.csv")
```

   Sorting the text column instead puts December before February, for the same reason `range()`
   misbehaved in Exercise 2.

# Exercise 4: the same data in XML

1. *Load the file with `xml2`. What kind of object did you get? Is it a data frame?*

```{r}
library(xml2)
doc <- read_xml("data/Air_Quality.xml")
class(doc)
xml_name(doc)
```

   Not a data frame: an object representing the XML tree, which holds everything we need but
   cannot be used as a table. The root element is called `row`.

2. *Collect the measurements with `xml_find_all(doc, "//row/row")` and count them. Compare the
   number with the number of rows in the CSV.*

   Each measurement is a `row` element inside a root that is also called `row`, which is why
   the XPath expression has `row` twice:

```{r}
rows <- xml_find_all(doc, "//row/row")
length(rows)
```

   16,122, the same as the CSV. The two files hold the same data in two formats.

3. *Inspect the first measurement: the names of its children, and their contents.*

   The children are the variables, their text is the values:

```{r}
xml_name(xml_children(rows[[1]]))
xml_text(xml_children(rows[[1]]))
```

4. *Extract one variable for all measurements with an XPath expression, for example every
   `data_value`. What type is the result, and what do you have to do before you can compute
   the mean?*

```{r}
data_value <- xml_text(xml_find_all(doc, "//row/row/data_value"))
length(data_value)
head(data_value, 5)
typeof(data_value)
```

   Text. XML has no column types, so everything arrives as character and you convert before
   computing:

```{r}
mean(as.numeric(data_value))
```

5. *Compare `start_date` here with `Start_Date` in the CSV, and the size of the two files with
   `file.size()`. What does XML give you that a CSV cannot, and what do you pay for it?*

```{r}
head(xml_text(xml_find_all(doc, "//row/row/start_date")), 2)
round(file.size("data/Air_Quality.xml") / 1024^2, 1)   # MB
round(file.size("data/Air_Quality.csv") / 1024^2, 1)   # MB
```

   The XML carries ISO timestamps, `2013-06-01T00:00:00`, which `readr` parses without a format
   string; the CSV has the ambiguous `06/01/2013`.

   XML stores structure: elements can be nested, repeated and labelled, every value carries its
   variable name, and a document can describe its own rules. A CSV holds a flat table and
   nothing else. You pay in size and speed, 8.7 MB against 1.9 MB for the same data, because
   every value is wrapped in its tags, and you need XPath to get anything out. For a flat
   table, the CSV is easier.

# Exercise 5: a file that is not comma separated

1. *Open `data/temp_anomaly.txt` in a text editor, or print its first lines from R. How many
   lines of metadata are there, and on which line does the first observation start?*

```{r}
readLines("data/temp_anomaly.txt", n = 12)
```

   Nine lines of metadata: variable, data set, file name, file path, bad flag, subset,
   longitude, latitude, and a line repeating the coordinates. The first observation,
   `JAN-1880`, is on line 10.

   The `\t` between the month and the value is the tab character, which is what `read_tsv()`
   uses as separator in question 2.

2. *Read the file with `read_tsv()`, `skip = 9` and `col_names = c("month", "temp_anomaly")`.*

```{r}
anomalies <- read_tsv("data/temp_anomaly.txt",
                      skip = 9,
                      col_names = c("month", "temp_anomaly"),
                      show_col_types = FALSE)
head(anomalies)
```

3. *What is the purpose of the `skip` argument, and why is it set to 9? And why does
   `col_names` have to be given here?*

   `skip = 9` drops the metadata before parsing starts, so it stays out of the table.
   `col_names` is needed because the first line after the metadata is already an observation:
   there is no header row to take the names from. Without it, `JAN-1880` and `0.33` would have
   become the column names and the series would be one observation short.

4. *Why do we use `read_tsv()` and not `read_csv()`? Try it with `read_csv()`: how many columns
   do you get, and what is inside them?*

   The separator is a tab, not a comma:

```{r}
anomalies_wrong <- read_csv("data/temp_anomaly.txt", skip = 9,
                            col_names = "everything", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(anomalies_wrong, 3)
```

   Finding no comma, `read_csv()` reads each line as a single field: one column, with the tab
   character `\t` still inside the values, and the anomaly as text instead of a number.
   `read_tsv()` is `read_csv()` with the tab as delimiter, and `read_delim()` takes any
   delimiter, which is what the `:` separated file in the Lecture 4 homework needs.

5. *How many observations does the series contain, and what is the mean anomaly?*

```{r}
nrow(anomalies)
mean(anomalies$temp_anomaly)
summary(anomalies$temp_anomaly)
```

   1713 monthly observations from January 1880 on, mean anomaly about 0.1 K, minimum $-1.78$,
   maximum $1.79$. The largest values are the recent ones.

# Exercise 6: what the browser shows and what the server sent

1. and 2. *Open the page, inspect the table, and say which tags hold the years and which hold
the party names.*

   The table is a `<table class="wikitable">`, and each Congress is one `<tr>`. Inside a row,
   the year and the party names each sit in their own `<td>`; the first row uses `<th>` for the
   column names. That regularity is what `html_table()` exploits in Exercise 7: rows become
   rows, cells become columns.

3. *Replace the `<h1>` title with one of your own. What happens on the screen?*

   The title changes immediately. The browser holds a copy of the document in memory, the DOM,
   and renders that copy; your edit changes the copy.

4. *Read the same page with R and print its first heading. Does your title appear? Why not?*

```{r eval=FALSE}
library(rvest)

doc <- read_html("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divided_government_in_the_United_States")
html_text(html_element(doc, "h1"))
```

```
[1] "Divided government in the United States"
```

   The real title comes back, not yours. `read_html()` asks Wikipedia's server for the page and
   parses the HTML the server sends; it never sees your browser. Your edit existed in one tab,
   on one computer.

5. *Reload the page. Where did your edit go, and who else saw it?*

   It is gone, and nobody saw it. Reloading throws the edited copy away and renders the
   document the server sends again.

6. *What does this tell you about the difference between what a website shows and what the data
behind it is?*

   A website is a rendering of text that a server sent you, and the rendering can be changed at
   will. Two consequences: the data behind a page is accessible, which is what makes Exercise 7
   possible, and a screenshot of a website is not evidence of anything.

# Additional exercises for training

## Exercise 7: scraping a table from a web page

*Build a CSV file with data on divided government in US politics out of the Wikipedia page on
[divided government in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divided_government_in_the_United_States):
fetch the page with `read_html()`, pick the table with `Year`, `President`, `Senate` and
`House`, drop the footnote row at the end, turn every range of years into one row per year,
remove Wikipedia's footnote markers, and write the result to `data/divided_gov.csv`.*

The code needs an internet connection, so it is shown here rather than executed.

```{r eval=FALSE}
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)

SOURCE_PATH <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divided_government_in_the_United_States"
OUTPUT_PATH <- "data/divided_gov.csv"

# 1. fetch the whole HTML document
doc <- read_html(SOURCE_PATH)

# 2. extract the tables and pick the right one
tables <- html_table(doc, fill = TRUE)
length(tables)
tab <- tables[[2]]        # the one with Year, President, Senate, House

# 3. check the last row and drop it if it is a footnote
tail(tab, 2)
tab <- tab[-nrow(tab), ]

# 4. one row per year instead of one row per Congress
all_years <- list()

for (i in seq_len(nrow(tab))) {
  row <- tab[i, ]
  pieces <- unlist(strsplit(row$Year, split = "[\\–\\-]", perl = TRUE))
  begin <- as.numeric(pieces[1])
  end <- as.numeric(pieces[2])

  all_years[[i]] <- data.frame(year = begin:(end - 1),
                               president = row$President,
                               senate = row$Senate,
                               house = row$House)
}

divided_gov <- bind_rows(all_years)

# 5. remove Wikipedia's footnote markers
divided_gov$senate <- str_remove_all(divided_gov$senate, "\\[[^\\]]*\\]")
divided_gov$house <- str_remove_all(divided_gov$house, "\\[[^\\]]*\\]")

# 6. inspect and write to disk
head(divided_gov)
write_csv(divided_gov, OUTPUT_PATH)
```

The result is also in the `data` folder:

```{r message=FALSE}
divided_gov <- readr::read_csv("data/divided_gov.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(divided_gov)
head(divided_gov, 4)
```

Three remarks on the method.

`html_table()` returns a list, because a page usually has more than one table, so you have to
look at the candidates and choose. `fill = TRUE` pads rows with fewer cells than the header,
which is common in hand-written Wikipedia tables.

The split pattern `"[\\–\\-]"` matches two characters, the ASCII hyphen `-` and the typographic
en dash `–`. Wikipedia uses both, and a pattern with only the hyphen fails on part of the rows
without saying so.

`begin:(end - 1)` and not `begin:end`: a Congress from 1861 to 1863 covers 1861 and 1862, and
1863 belongs to the next one. Off-by-one errors are the usual mistake when reshaping periods
into years, and the way to catch them is to count a couple of rows by hand.
